summary: Christine Jones argues that soil restoration, meaning improving soil structure, microbial life, nutrient density and carbon levels, begins with photosynthesis. The article documents nutrient declines in food over 70 years, explains the plant-microbe bridge and the soil carbon sink, and sets out five principles: keep green cover year-round, value microbes, embrace diversity, avoid chemical overuse, and avoid aggressive tillage. It concludes that agricultural and garden soils should become net carbon sinks.
one_line: Christine Jones outlines five principles for restoring soil health, carbon storage and food nutrient density through photosynthesis, microbes, diversity and reduced chemical and tillage use.
key_facts: Nutrient levels in almost every kind of food have fallen by between 10 and 100 percent in the past 70 years.
Over the last 150 years, many of the world's prime agricultural soils have lost between 30 and 75 percent of their carbon.
Around 30 percent of the world's cropland has been abandoned in the last 40 years due to soil decline.
Between 1940 and 1991, copper declined by 76% in vegetables and by 24% in meat, according to Dr. David Thomas's analysis.
Around 85 to 90 percent of plant nutrient acquisition is microbially-mediated.
Only 10 to 40 percent of applied nitrogen fertilizer is taken up by plants, meaning 60 to 90 percent is lost through volatilization and leaching.
At least 80 percent of applied water-soluble phosphorus rapidly adsorbs to aluminium and iron oxides or forms calcium, aluminum, or iron phosphates.
Only 10-15 percent of fertilizer P is taken up by crops and pastures in the year of application.
Mycorrhizal fungi can supply up to 90 percent of plants' nitrogen (N) and phosphorous (P) requirements.
Nitrous oxide has almost 300 times the global warming potential of carbon dioxide.
Organic carbon holds between four and 20 times its own weight in water.
Figure 1 notes that growth of both tops and roots is significantly impaired if more than 50 percent of the green leaf is removed in a single grazing event.
On average, global cropland is bare for around half of every year.

An increase of around 5 percent in global photosynthetic capacity and/or photosynthetic rate would be sufficient to counter the CO2 flux from the burning of fossil fuels, provided the extra carbon was sequestered in soil in a stable form.
Innovative farmers are experimenting with up to 70 different plant species to see which combinations perform best for soil restoration.
